newsitem.title: USA: Motorola cellular woes seen most damaging.
newsitem.headline: Motorola cellular woes seen most damaging.

text.p: Motorola Inc's difficulties in the cellular phone and pager businesses may be even more damaging to the company than weakness in the semiconductor industry, securities analysts said Wednesday.

Cellular competition will pressure prices long-term, while Motorola's semiconductor business will likely turn around with the industry in the medium term, analysts said. However, with about 18 to 20 percent of Motorola's semiconductors used in its own products, Motorola will see less gain than other players when that industry does improve, they noted.

"The cellular handset pricing competition continues to be strong and ferocious as analog spills over into digital, specifically in the GSM (global system of mobile communications) area," said Rakesh Sood, an analyst for Hambrecht & Quist.
"Our expectation is (the competition) will continue for some time," he said.

Earlier Wednesday, Schaumburg, Ill.-based Motorola projected a "significant drop" in third quarter earnings, which the company later said may mean a decline of 25 percent or more versus second quarter results.

According to analysts, Motorola's general systems sector (which includes cellular phones and pagers) made up about 40 percent of total revenues last quarter, while semiconductors accounted for about 29 percent.
Analysts agreed Motorola may cut operating costs further, and one said it may even have to restructure. In July Motorola was forced to lay off employees for the first time in more than a decade.
"I'm virtually convinced there will actually be people laid off," said Scott Wright, an analyst for Argus Research, who has followed the company for about two years.
"I wouldn't be surprised to hear more specific news on the restructuring front," he said.

Many analysts said they were surprised by the magnitude of impact the cellular and paging competition is having on Motorola. They pointed to international markets, typically solid ground for the company, where market share is eroding.
Motorola said its overall market share in handsets has declined this year and analysts said the trend will continue.
"It's increasingly a consumer electronics business and market share of 25 to 30 percent is pretty good," said Matthew Robison, an analyst with Montgomery Securities.
Motorola now has an estimated market share of 35 to 40 percent worldwide and 45 to 50 percent domestically, he said.

Even Motorola's CDMA (code division multiple access) wireless phone technology is likely to face stiff competition. Many of the cell phone manufacturers Motorola has licensed the technology to are producing phones faster than Motorola.
The CDMA roll-out is still underway and Motorola's CDMA phones are not expected to be manufactured full-force before mid-1997, analysts said.

"In fact the Koreans are already in high-volume and Motorola is not, so there is very little upside in that part of the story," Robison said. "When you look at the aggregate wireless business having tough comparisons there, I don't see anything that's going to really change that."

The weakness in Motorola's cellular and paging business ripples into its already struggling semiconductor sector, analysts said. The industry as a whole got a boost from a slight rise in the August book-to-bill ratio, but analysts said Motorola will see a less dramatic increase because it is its own key customer.
